1:
Whoever divided the chapters made a foolish division here, interrupting the sequence, for what follows continues the apostle's explanation and the verb should be read as a pluperfect, I had determined. Calvin presses that reading, and Ellicott agrees the break is obviously wrong, adding that he determined for himself, consulting his own feelings as well as theirs. Gill adds that he is also clearing himself of the charge of levity. Clarke and Barnes put the reason in the state of the church: had he come while the scandals stood unpunished he must have used his authority, and Clarke says roundly that he resolved not to see them at all until the evils were put away. Calvin's account is gentler: he had already come once by an epistle and pained them severely, and would not come again while they were unrepentant, choosing rather to allow them longer time. Robertson raises the question the others pass over: what does again mean? Either Paul had made a second, sorrowful visit besides the one recorded in Acts, or, having had one joyful visit, he did not wish the second to be in grief; the Greek allows both, and there is no way to tell.

The second verse turns on a paradox, and Robertson marks the particle carrying it: the conjunction accepts the condition, the verb for making sorry matched by one of the same causative form for making glad. Barnes states the sense plainly: had he come and been called to inflict discipline, the whole church would have been in grief, and none left to comfort him but the very people he had just grieved; such was his sympathy that he could not be happy unless they were. Ellicott finds the force of the opening conjunction lying below the surface. It might have been said, and perhaps was, that he had not minded giving pain when he wrote; his answer is that the man on whom the pain falls is thereby given the power of making him glad. He adds that the abruptness and the singular number show the one great offender standing before the apostle's eye. Wesley reduces it to a sentence, that he cannot be comforted till that man's grief is removed; Clarke, that he could not rejoice to see those he loved in distress. Calvin draws a pastoral rule from it: no one willingly makes sorrow for himself, and if this temper prevailed among pastors it would restrain them from terrifying minds they ought rather to encourage.

What the same thing was that he wrote is disputed only at the edges. Gill and Barnes refer it to the former epistle and the sentence passed there on the incestuous man, Barnes including the general orders to reform the abuses; Ellicott notes that the pronoun points to nothing actually said, showing how sharply certain passages stood in his memory. Robertson alone asks whether the tense may be epistolary and mean the present letter, decides against it from the context and the seventh chapter, then cannot say which is meant, since what follows can hardly apply to the first epistle and may point to one now lost. On the fourth verse they agree. Clarke says his enemies had painted him austere, better pleased to wound than to heal; Barnes suspects the same charge and answers that the letter was written weeping, adding that admonition is always rightly given if given with tears, and that few who reprove do so. Calvin is harder still on the noisy reprover who fulminates against vice while at ease in his own mind, and holds it the part of a pastor to weep inwardly before calling others to weep. Robertson and Ellicott gloss the word for anguish as a constriction of the heart, Ellicott suspecting a medical term. Henry's note is that even censure is a way of showing love, and that pain should be given unwillingly.
5:
The fifth verse is broken by a qualifying clause, and the ambiguity is real. Ellicott sets out three constructions and prefers the first, that the offender grieved not the apostle only but, to some extent, the whole church, which was in truth the chief sufferer; and he notes the pronoun stands first in the Greek and is emphatic. Clarke refers the phrase to the people rather than the degree of grief, since only a part had caused him pain and it would be unreasonable to load the rest with blame belonging to that party. Calvin prefers the reading of Chrysostom, who takes the words as one continuous sentence, and dismisses another, which makes the qualification mean a part of the saints only, as more ingenious than solid. Robertson notes scholars are divided whether the man is the offender of the earlier letter or the ringleader of the opposition, the delicacy of not naming him being the same either way. Gill takes the conditional as concession, not doubt, and Henry adds that some of them were still puffed up and had not mourned.

What the punishment was, and who imposed it, occupies the sixth verse. Ellicott would render the word censure or rebuke, since it differs from the ordinary terms for punishment, and reconstructs the sequence: a meeting of the church, the man delivered over, and almost certainly exclusion from religious and social fellowship. He then presses the phrase rendered of many, which means by the majority, and infers that the vote had not been unanimous, the minority being either those who resented the apostle's dictation or those who boasted of their freedom. Robertson agrees the sense is the majority, and adds that if the earlier letter is in view they had taken the advice and expelled the man. Barnes resists that reading. The words cannot describe a single bishop or a bench of elders, and though Locke and Macknight give the majority, he prefers the plain force of the expression, that the whole assembled society acted, adding that a single early example makes no binding rule. Wesley agrees the whole congregation acquiesced and not the rulers only, and remarks how tenderly the offender is handled, since neither his name nor his crime is so much as mentioned. Gill and Clarke are content the censure has done its work.

The remedy follows, and the danger is what makes it urgent. Ellicott says the apostle's indignation has passed, on hearing of the man's state, into pity and anxiety, despair and madness and apostasy seeming to float before his mind. Robertson glosses the verb as drinking down, and the word for confirm as a legal term meaning to ratify, found in the New Testament only here and once in Galatians. Ellicott and Clarke take that force: the restoration was to be as formal and public as the rebuke had been, a collective ratification of a love that had never ceased, since it was for the credit of the gospel that they had cut him off. Calvin states the principle most exactly. The end of excommunication is that the offender, overpowered by a sense of his sin, should be humbled and seek pardon; a man brought that far needs consolation rather than reproof, and to press him further is not discipline but cruel domineering, nothing being more dangerous than to hand Satan a weapon by leaving a penitent without comfort. He turns the same rule against the ancient canons that imposed three years, seven years, or a whole lifetime of exclusion, which either drive a man further off or teach him hypocrisy. Barnes insists the restoration is favour and not right, and that the offence should be buried rather than raked over; Henry, that comfort depends on reconciliation with those scandalised, the design being to reform and not to ruin; Gill, that the censure has lain on him long enough.
9:
The ninth verse gives another reason, and its reference is disputed. Ellicott notes the tense may be epistolary and settles nothing, then offers two readings: the present letter, written to see whether they are as obedient now as before, or the earlier one, whose directions were meant partly as a test. He prefers the first, since it scarcely seems like the apostle to make punishment a trial of obedience, and finds a subtle delicacy in the suggestion that, having obeyed in punishing, they should obey in forgiving. Barnes denies that obedience was the only aim, or that anyone was asked to do a wrong thing to prove himself; writing rather than coming in person gave them opportunity to show themselves willing, and every object has now been gained. Robertson glosses the noun as proof by testing, a late word the New Testament has from this writer only, and the adjective as from a verb meaning to give ear. Calvin hears an objection behind the verse: from so stern a judge to become all at once a defender looks like a man swayed by conflicting dispositions. His answer is that he obtained what he asked, and being satisfied must give way to compassion.

The tenth verse joins the apostle's vote to theirs. Gill takes the promise widely, as covering anyone in any case, though this man is chiefly meant, and granted on their account. Barnes reads it as confidence in them as a society: if they forgive, he approves and forgives with them. Calvin puts it as an undertaking in advance, that he subscribes their sentence of pardon before it is passed. Then comes the phrase rendered in the person of Christ, which every one of them handles. Robertson makes it more exactly in the presence of Christ, before his face. Ellicott allows that rendering but thinks the English right, a stronger form of the phrase in the name of the Lord Jesus used earlier, so that the absolution is as authoritative as the censure, the apostolic power of remission claimed in its fulness. Barnes collects the older renderings, and after tracing the word from the part around the eye to the face and then to presence, settles on acting under Christ's eye and accountable to him. Calvin knows the lieutenant reading and declines it, preferring to hear the apostle say that he forgives sincerely and without pretence. Clarke makes it a rule: as Christ deals with the penitent, so let the church.

The last verse turns to the adversary, the figure commercial or military by turns. Robertson derives the verb from the covetous man, to overreach, the word for devices being used especially of evil designs. Gill keeps the trading figure and lists how the advantage is gained: when discipline is brought into contempt or turned into tyranny, or a member driven out, so that the church loses one who might have been useful and the enemy gains him. Ellicott changes it to a game against the Tempter in which souls are both counters and stake; the last move had been to deliver the sinner over, and if the answer is a temptation to despair, stratagem must be met by strategy. Clarke fears for the credit of discipline itself, since if the penitent is not restored it will be represented as destroying rather than mending, and the enemies of the ministry will say so gladly. Barnes warns that under pretence of duty the church may be drawn into needless severity and an unforgiving spirit, its best efforts liable to be turned against it. Calvin reports the reading that refers the danger to the offender, swallowed up in a gulf of despair, but prefers to refer it to the apostle and the church, and to the strife that would have arisen had he not met their wishes. Wesley remembers that the loss of one soul is a common loss.
12:
Chrysostom raises two questions before anything in the verses is explained: they seem unworthy of the apostle, if for a brother's absence he threw away so great an opportunity of saving men, and they seem to hang apart from what goes before. He answers the second by recalling the affliction in Asia with which the letter opened, so that the failure to find Titus is one more affliction in that series, and he adds why it weighed so much: trials are fearful enough to endure, but when there is nobody to comfort and help bear the burden the tempest becomes greater. Henry and Ellicott mark the same seam from the other side. Ellicott treats the business of the offender as the parenthesis and this as the resumed narrative; Henry treats the resumed narrative as itself the digression, and reckons it to run on for four chapters more. Barnes settles it on the particle, which is properly adversative but often merely transitional, and here continues the account of his affection for them. Gill hears a second purpose in the turn, the apostle now moving to answer a charge of insincerity in his preaching.

On Troas itself they supply what the verse omits. Barnes places it in Phrygia or Mysia on the Hellespont, on the regular route from Ephesus to Macedonia, taken because he had resolved not to go to Corinth; Gill adds only that it lay in the lesser Asia and had once been Troy. Ellicott thinks the article may point to the district rather than the city, and judges that a church there had probably been founded by Luke, since the first visit was of a few days and left no trace of preaching, though a flourishing community existed months later. Robertson observes that Luke records two visits to Troas but not this one, and puts the difficulty of the passage in a sentence: here was an open door that he could not enter. The open door itself is common property. Clarke and Henry take it for liberty and success together, Henry adding that as the apostle opened his mouth freely God opened the hearers' hearts, as he opened the heart of Lydia. Calvin gives the metaphor its history, citing a rabbinic use of gate in the same sense and the remark that the angel questioned Hagar to give her an opening to speak, and draws the rule: where a door stands open we are invited in, and where it is shut we should go elsewhere rather than weary ourselves.

Then the door is left standing open and he goes. Gill dwells on the plain humanity of it: a man so great was but a man, of like passions with others, too uneasy to be satisfied to stay. Robertson finds the same thing in the tense, which is not to be flattened into a simple past, the shadow of that restlessness being still on him as he writes; he glosses the noun as a letting up, and the parting as a verb that came to mean bidding adieu. Ellicott reconstructs the arrangement that failed: Titus had been sent to learn what the first letter had done and was to meet him at Troas, and when he was not there the apostle pressed on to Macedonia, probably by way of Philippi, where Luke was and where the two most likely met. Clarke confirms that Titus came at last with a joyful account, and Wesley explains the restlessness by the one desire to know how the letter had been received. Barnes and Calvin both feel the difficulty. Barnes notes how rarely this man left an inviting field with every prospect, and allows that there are cases where a minister should. Calvin puts the objection sharply, that an open door is itself evidence of a divine call, and answers it as Chrysostom does, from the strength of his attachment to this church.
14:
The thanksgiving breaks in abruptly, and its reason lies outside the sentence. Ellicott finds it in what was passing through the writer's memory, Titus having come like a courier with news of a victory; Barnes lists three causes: that Titus came, that the letter had done its work, and that Macedonia prospered, so that the forced removal from Troas turned to joy. Calvin guards the motive: the boast is not ambition, nor the Pharisee's thanksgiving, but a wish that whatever is praiseworthy be seen as God's work, made for the readers' sake, that a ministry God honoured elsewhere not be wasted among them. Then the verb divides them. Ellicott says there is no authority for the causative sense the English gives it, renders it who always leads us in his triumph, and adds that it would be unlike this writer to cast himself as the victorious commander; Robertson agrees no example of the causative has been found, and paints him instead as a captive in the procession. Barnes and Calvin take the other view, that the form is causative and God makes us to triumph; Calvin sets the apostle beside the chariot as a lieutenant sharing the honour, and Clarke reads a victory so complete it ruins the enemy.

The procession itself they reconstruct between them. Clarke is fullest: the senate granted the honour only for a signal victory, the general in a purple robe interwoven with gold, carried in an ivory chariot behind two white horses, with carts of spoil and captive kings in chains behind, and a slave at his back reciting his vices to keep him humble, while every temple stood open and every altar smoked. Ellicott adds the route along the sacred way, and the grim moment at the foot of the Capitol where some prisoners were led to execution and others pardoned; and he remarks that the writer had never seen such a thing, and must have had it from Roman soldiers or Jews of the imperial household. Robertson and Calvin both fix on the perfume, Robertson on the garlands and incense bearers, Calvin citing a description of streets and temples full of incense, the one smell being death to the vanquished and life to the conquerors. Clarke notes that Corinth of all cities knew what a triumph was, having furnished one two centuries before when the consul destroyed her, and that this one was of a wholly different kind.

The figure then transfers to the persons of the preachers. Gill denies they are fragrant in themselves, having the same corrupt hearts as other men, and traces the image to the anointing oil that ran from Aaron's head to his garments' skirts; Barnes hears rather the incense of the sacrifices, and insists that what God accepts is not the success but the fidelity. Calvin states the hard half plainly, that both odours are grateful to God, the one by which the elect are refreshed and the one from which the wicked receive a deadly shock, so that a preacher whose success falls short of his desire may know that what is an offensive smell to the world is fragrance to God. On the double effect, Clarke and Barnes both quote the rabbinic sayings that the words of the law were a savour of life to Israel and of death to the peoples of the world, and that the bee brings honey to its owner but stings others; Robertson says shortly that some are actually hardened by preaching. Ellicott keeps the incense in view, a breath from Paradise to the one class and a charnel-house sweetness to the other. On the closing question they agree no man is sufficient of himself. Wesley answers in a line, none but by the power of God's Spirit; Calvin reports two older readings and prefers a third, an implied contrast: the profession is common, the reality very thin sown.
17:
The comparison is with a majority, and that is the first thing noticed. Ellicott would render it not as most, the greater number, and hears a ring of sadness in it, since even then the ways of error were manifold and the way of truth one; among Judaisers, seekers after Greek wisdom, men who called licence liberty and men who questioned the resurrection, few preached the true word in its purity. Gill takes the number as part of the description, great swarms of false teachers having risen in the earliest times, and notes that some copies, with the Syriac and Arabic, read as the rest. Barnes widens the reference beyond one city to all who mingle human philosophy or tradition with the pure word. Calvin makes an observation the others do not. He does not think it likely the men reproved preached openly false doctrine at all; his opinion is that they corrupted the right use of doctrine for gain or ambition, and so emptied it of its energy, adding that the boast is made only because proof could be demanded of it.

The verb itself then occupies them, and it is a trader's word. Robertson derives it from the huckster or pedlar, a term common in every stage of the language, and remarks how such men were suspected of laying the best fruit on top. Clarke and Barnes both make him a vintner, notorious for thinning good wine with worthless liquor to increase the quantity and selling it at the price of the pure, and both cite the Greek of Isaiah, thy vintners mix thy wine with water; Barnes adds that of all commodities wine offers the readiest opening for such tricks. Wesley puts it in a clause, that they mix the wine with baser liquors. Clarke extends the sense to any prostitution of what is right for gain, quoting the phrases for making peace and making war for money, and a comic poet who used the word of an old woman patched and painted, whose wrinkled face would show if the paint were washed off. Calvin follows the same trail to a historian's jibe that a certain king was a huckster because he retailed everything, and reports that the word properly means a retailer, one who deals at second hand. Barnes notices that the old English version rendered it choppe and chaunge with the word of God, calls the idea beautiful, and thinks it a rare place where that translator missed the sense.

How the adulteration is done is where they become useful. Calvin distinguishes two ways. Doctrine is corrupted when mixed with falsehood, so that what is commended under the name is no longer genuine; and when, keeping its purity, it is turned this way and that to please men. There will be found some, he says, in whose teaching no impiety can be detected, yet who hunt applause by a display of acuteness and eloquence, or are ambitious of a place, or gape after gain, and so make the doctrine subservient to their own inclinations, playing with the sacred word as with a ball. Barnes lists the philosophical forms of the fault: attaching an explanation to a revealed fact until the theory matters as much as the fact, explaining away whatever offends, and forcing the record to agree with prevailing opinion by an interpretation that can make it mean anything. His verdict is severe, that persecution left the gospel pure while philosophy dimmed its lustre. Against all this stand four clauses, whose weight Robertson marks: from God, in his sight, in Christ. Ellicott observes that sincerity alone would rest too much on the man's own consciousness, since he could not be sure of it unless he knew it was given him. Wesley says the tongue is ours but the power is God's, and Clarke that the conscience which convicts the vintner acquits the preacher here.
